{{short description|Gives a lower bound on the number of lines determined by n points in a projective plane}}
{{about|the number of lines determined by a finite set of points|coloring infinite graphs|De Bruijn–Erdős theorem (graph theory)}}

In [[incidence geometry]], the '''De Bruijn–Erdős theorem''', originally published by [[Nicolaas Govert de Bruijn]] and [[Paul Erdős]] in 1948,<ref name=dbe>{{citation | last1 = De Bruijn | first1 = N. G. | author1-link = Nicolaas Govert de Bruijn | last2 = Erdős | first2 = P.| author2-link = Paul Erdős| title = On a {{sic|combina|tioral|nolink=y}} problem | journal = Indagationes Mathematicae | year = 1948 | volume = 10 | pages = 421–423 | url = http://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1948-01.pdf }}</ref> states a [[lower bound]] on the number of lines determined by ''n'' points in a [[projective plane]]. By [[Duality (projective geometry)|duality]], this is also a bound on the number of intersection points determined by a configuration of lines.<ref name=batten>{{citation |last1=Batten|first1=Lynn Margaret|author-link=Lynn Batten|title= Combinatorics of Finite Geometries |title-link= Combinatorics of Finite Geometries |year=1997|publisher=Cambridge University Press|edition=2nd|isbn=0-521-59014-0|chapter=2.2 The De Bruijn–Erdős theorem|pages=25&ndash;27}}</ref>

Although the proof given by De Bruijn and Erdős is [[Combinatorial proof|combinatorial]], De Bruijn and Erdős noted in their paper that the analogous ([[Euclidean geometry|Euclidean]]) result is a consequence of the  [[Sylvester–Gallai theorem]], by an [[Mathematical induction|induction]] on the number of points.<ref name=dbe/>

==Statement of the theorem==
[[File:Nearpencil.svg|thumb|A near-pencil on seven points]]
Let ''P'' be a configuration of ''n'' points in a projective plane, not all on a line. Let ''t'' be the number of lines determined by&nbsp;''P''. Then,
* ''t'' ≥ ''n'', and
* if ''t'' = ''n'', any two lines have exactly one point of ''P'' in common. In this case, ''P'' is either a projective plane or ''P'' is a ''near pencil'', meaning that exactly ''n'' - 1 of the points are [[collinear]].<ref name=batten/>

==Euclidean proof==
The theorem is clearly true for three non-collinear points. We proceed by [[Mathematical induction|induction]].

Assume ''n''&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;3 and the theorem is true for ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1.
Let ''P'' be a set of ''n'' points not all collinear.
The [[Sylvester–Gallai theorem]] states that there is a line containing exactly two points of ''P''. Such two point lines are called ''ordinary lines''.
Let ''a'' and ''b'' be the two points of ''P'' on an ordinary line.

If the removal of point ''a'' produces a set of collinear points then ''P'' generates a near pencil of ''n'' lines (the ''n'' - 1 ordinary lines through ''a'' plus the one line containing the other ''n'' - 1 points).

Otherwise, the removal of ''a'' produces a set, ''P' '', of ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 points that are not all collinear.
By the induction hypothesis, ''P' '' determines at least ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 lines. The ordinary line determined by ''a'' and ''b'' is not among these, so ''P'' determines at least ''n'' lines.

==J. H. Conway's proof==
[[John Horton Conway]] has a purely combinatorial proof which consequently also holds for points and lines over the [[complex numbers]], [[quaternions]] and [[octonions]].<ref>Stasys Jukna, ''Extremal Combinatorics'', Second edition, Springer Verlag, 2011, pages 167 - 168.</ref>
